intro: Angels appear on greeting cards, tree ornaments and paintings. Most of those pictures show sweet babies with tiny wings. The Bible describes something very different. Its messengers are often strong and bright. People who meet them are told, "Do not be afraid."

In this unit you will read what the Bible says about angels, with Michael Heiser as your guide. Heiser was a scholar who read the Bible in Hebrew and Greek. You will learn the words for messengers, cherubim and seraphim. You will meet Michael, Gabriel and Raphael. Then you will meet a puzzling figure. He is called the Angel of the LORD, and he speaks as if he were God.

By the end, you will be able to explain what the word angel means. You will be able to retell the stories of Hagar, Moses, Gideon and Samson's parents. You will be able to describe Heiser's reading of the Angel of the LORD. You will also know at least one other way readers understand him.
bigQuestion: What does the Bible say angels are and do, and who is the Angel of the LORD who speaks as God?

timeline.t: Isaiah has his vision of the seraphim, in the year King Uzziah dies (Isaiah 6)
The Torah is put into Greek; the Hebrew mal'ak becomes angelos
The Book of Tobit, with the angel Raphael, is written
Luke and Hebrews are written; Gabriel visits Mary, and angels are called spirits who serve
Justin Martyr links the Angel of the LORD with the Son of God
The Mishnah is written down, including the rule that an agent is like the sender
Augustine writes that God may have spoken through created angels
Raphael paints little winged children, part of a trend that made baby angels popular
The King James Version of the Bible is published in English
Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm, with his two Yahwehs reading
Heiser publishes Angels, explaining that angel names a job
Michael Heiser dies; his books and podcast are still widely read and heard

words.d: a Hebrew word that means messenger, used for human and heavenly messengers
a Greek word that means messenger; the English word angel comes from it
a Bible name for heavenly beings, picturing them as members of God's household
the great crowd or army of heavenly beings around God's throne
powerful winged guardians of holy places, like Eden and the ark of the covenant
six-winged beings above God's throne in Isaiah 6 who call out that God is holy
a chief messenger; Jude 9 uses this title for Michael
books, like Tobit, that Protestants keep outside their canon but Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include
a figure in the Hebrew Bible who is sent by God but often speaks as God
the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often printed LORD in English Bibles
Heiser's reading: God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD
someone sent to act or speak for another; the Mishnah says an agent is like the sender

test.q: What do the Hebrew word mal'ak and the Greek word angelos both mean?
test.why: Both words mean messenger. Heiser stressed that angel names a job, not a kind of being.

test.q: In Genesis 32, who does the Hebrew word mal'ak describe?
choices: Both heavenly messengers and Jacob's human messengers
test.why: Genesis 32:1 uses mal'ak for messengers of God, and 32:3 uses it for the men Jacob sends to Esau.

test.q: Which beings sit on the cover of the ark of the covenant?
test.why: Exodus 25:18–22 describes two gold cherubim on the ark's cover.

test.q: Which beings in Isaiah 6 have six wings?
test.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

test.q: Which angel is called the great prince in Daniel 12:1?
test.why: Daniel 12:1 calls Michael the great prince who stands up for Daniel's people.

test.q: In which Bibles is the Book of Tobit part of the Old Testament?
test.why: Tobit is in Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments. Protestants place it in the Apocrypha.

test.q: Where did the picture of chubby baby angels mostly come from?
choices: European paintings made long after the Bible
test.why: Painters in Italy, about five hundred years ago, made winged children popular. Bible angels often look like grown men.

test.q: Which verse describes angels as spirits who serve, sent to help?
test.why: Hebrews 1:14 calls angels serving spirits sent to help people.

test.q: What did Elisha's servant see when his eyes were opened in 2 Kings 6?
test.why: 2 Kings 6:17 says he saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

test.q: In Genesis 16, what does Hagar call the one who spoke to her?
test.why: Genesis 16:13 says she called the LORD who spoke to her the God who sees me.

test.q: In Judges 6, what happens right after the angel greets Gideon?
choices: The text says the LORD turned to him and spoke
test.why: Judges 6:14 says the LORD turned to Gideon, right after the angel of the LORD had spoken.

test.q: What did Heiser mean by the two Yahwehs?
choices: Two gods of two different nations
God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD
Two names for the angel Gabriel
Two copies of the Hebrew Bible
test.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser described God unseen and God seen as two Yahwehs.

test.q: What does Exodus 23:21 say is in the angel God sends?
test.why: Exodus 23:21 says, My name is in him.

test.q: How do Jewish readers usually explain the angel of the LORD?
choices: As a messenger or agent who speaks for God
test.why: Jewish readers usually see him as a messenger. The Mishnah teaches that an agent is like the one who sends him.

test.q: How did Augustine's view differ from Justin Martyr's?
choices: Augustine thought God may have spoken through created angels
Augustine rejected the Book of Genesis
Augustine said the angel was Gideon
test.why: Justin linked the appearances to the Son of God. Augustine thought God may have spoken through created angels.

write.prompt: Who is the Angel of the LORD? Choose two or three passages from this unit, such as Genesis 16:7–13, Exodus 3:2–6, Judges 6:11–24 or Exodus 23:20–21. Explain what each passage says. Then explain how Heiser read the Angel and how Jewish readers or another Christian reader, like Augustine, understood him.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Say who holds each view: Heiser argues, Jewish readers explain, Augustine thought.
Compare the readings fairly. You do not need to pick a winner.
Use unit words like mal'ak, angel of the LORD, agent and two Yahwehs.

title: Angels and the Angel of the LORD

chapters.title: What Angels Are and What They Do
chapters.bigQuestion: What does the Bible mean by the word angel, and what do the angels in its stories do?

story.title: The Angel on the Tree
story.kicker: A small ornament with chubby cheeks starts a big question about what the Bible really says.
paragraphs: Marcus hung the last ornament on his grandmother's tree. It was a tiny angel. It had round pink cheeks, curly hair and two little wings. "Angels are so cute," Marcus said. His grandmother smiled. She sat down with her Bible and opened it to the Gospel of Luke.

She read about shepherds out in the fields at night. An angel of the Lord suddenly stood near them. A bright light shone all around. Luke says the shepherds were terrified. The very first thing the angel said to them was, "Do not be afraid."

Marcus looked at the ornament again. "Why would anyone be scared of this?" he asked. His grandmother laughed. She said the angels in Bible stories do not look like babies. When they show up, people often fall to the ground or shake. In the Book of Daniel, a messenger comes, and Daniel falls on his face.

"So where did baby angels come from?" Marcus asked. His grandmother said that painters in Italy, about five hundred years ago, loved to paint little children with wings. People liked those pictures very much. Over time, many people began to picture all angels that way.

Marcus wanted to know more. He found out about a scholar named Michael Heiser. Heiser studied the Bible in its old languages, Hebrew and Greek. He wrote a whole book called Angels (2018) about what the Bible says about them. Marcus decided to start there.
story.think: Why do you think angels in Bible stories so often begin by saying "Do not be afraid"?

lessons.title: Angel Means Messenger
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word mal'ak and the Greek word angelos both mean messenger, so the word angel names a job.
reading: In Genesis 32, Jacob is traveling home. He is nervous about meeting his brother Esau. So he sends some people ahead with a message. The Hebrew word for these people is *mal'ak*. It means messenger. These messengers were ordinary men from Jacob's own camp.

The same word shows up just two verses earlier. In Genesis 32:1, messengers of God meet Jacob on the road. Those are heavenly messengers. Hebrew uses one word for both groups. A messenger is anyone who is sent with a message, whoever sends him.

Long ago, the Hebrew Bible was put into Greek. Then mal'ak became *angelos*. The English word angel comes from angelos. Michael Heiser stressed this point in his book Angels (2018). He said angel names a job. It tells you what someone does, not what kind of being they are.

words.d: a Hebrew word that means messenger; it is used for human messengers and for heavenly ones
a Greek word that means messenger; the English word angel comes from it

look.title: Two Kinds of Messengers
look.text: Genesis 32:1 — Jacob goes on his way, and messengers of God meet him. Genesis 32:3 — Jacob sends messengers ahead to his brother Esau in the land of Edom. In Hebrew, both verses use the same word: mal'ak.
look.prompt: Both groups are called mal'ak. What clues in each verse tell you which messengers are heavenly and which are human?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word mal'ak mean?
check.why: Mal'ak means messenger. The Bible uses it for human messengers and for heavenly ones.

check.q: In Genesis 32:3, who are the messengers Jacob sends to Esau?
check.why: Jacob sends ordinary men ahead to his brother. The Hebrew still calls them mal'ak, messengers.

check.q: According to Heiser, what does the word angel tell you?
check.why: In Angels (2018), Heiser explained that angel names a job: carrying a message. It does not describe a kind of being.

lessons.title: Many Names for One Family
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible also calls heavenly beings sons of God, holy ones and the host of heaven; Heiser said these names describe what they are.
reading: If angel is a job, who does the job? The Bible uses several names for the beings of the unseen world. In Job 38:7, God says the *sons of God* shouted for joy when the earth was made. That is a family word. It pictures heavenly beings who belong to God's household.

Psalm 89:5–7 calls them the *holy ones*. They gather in a great meeting around God. In 1 Kings 22:19, the prophet Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne. All the *host of heaven* stands beside him. Host is an old word for a very large army or crowd.

Heiser thought these names describe what the beings are. They are spirit beings who live in God's presence. Mal'ak describes one thing some of them do, which is carry messages. In his view, a son of God could be sent with a message. Then he would be doing the job of an angel.

words.d: a Bible name for heavenly beings, picturing them as members of God's household
a Bible name for heavenly beings who gather around God, as in Psalm 89
the great crowd or army of heavenly beings around God's throne

look.title: What Micaiah Saw
look.text: Micaiah said: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne. The whole army of heaven was standing around him, on his right side and on his left.
look.cite: 1 Kings 22:19, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What picture of God does this verse give? Who is standing near the throne, and where?

check.q: Which name pictures heavenly beings as members of God's household?
check.why: Sons of God is a family name. Job 38:7 uses it for heavenly beings who shouted for joy at creation.

check.q: In 1 Kings 22:19, what does Micaiah see around the LORD's throne?
choices: Two gold cherubim on a box
check.why: Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with all the host of heaven standing beside him.

check.q: How did Heiser think names like holy ones differ from mal'ak?
choices: They say what the beings are; mal'ak says what they do
They are only used for human beings
They come from paintings, not the Bible
They mean exactly the same as mal'ak
check.why: Heiser said names like sons of God and holy ones describe the beings. Mal'ak, messenger, describes a job.

lessons.title: Cherubim Guard Holy Places
lessons.mainIdea: In the Bible, cherubim are powerful guardians of holy places, like the garden of Eden and the ark of the covenant.
reading: At the end of Genesis 3, Adam and Eve must leave the garden of Eden. God places *cherubim* on the east side of the garden. A flaming sword turns every way. Their job is to guard the path to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). Cherubim is the plural of cherub.

Cherubim show up again in Exodus 25. God tells Moses to make a gold-covered box called the *ark of the covenant*. On its cover sit two gold cherubim. They face each other, and their wings spread over the top. God says he will speak to Moses from between them (Exodus 25:22).

Ezekiel 10 describes cherubim with four faces and many eyes. They are not babies at all. Heiser noted that in the Bible, cherubim guard God's throne and holy places. Scholars also point out that ancient kings in Assyria set huge winged guardian statues at their palace gates.

words.d: powerful winged guardians in the Bible; the word is the plural of cherub
the gold-covered box described in Exodus 25, with two gold cherubim on its cover

look.title: Picture the Ark
look.text: Picture a wooden box covered in gold. It is a little longer than a grown-up's arm. On its lid kneel two gold cherubim. They face each other and look down. Their wings reach forward and almost touch. Exodus 25:22 says God will meet Moses and speak from the space between them.
look.prompt: Why might the writer place guardians exactly where God is said to speak? What do guards usually protect?

check.q: In Genesis 3:24, what do the cherubim guard?
choices: The path to the tree of life
check.why: Genesis 3:24 says cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life.

check.q: Where did two gold cherubim sit, according to Exodus 25?
choices: On the cover of the ark of the covenant
On the branches of the tree of life
check.why: Exodus 25:18–22 places two gold cherubim on the ark's cover, facing each other.

check.q: What do cherubim mostly do in the Bible?
choices: Guard God's throne and holy places
Sing Holy, holy, holy in Isaiah 6
check.why: Cherubim guard holy places. The ones who sing Holy, holy, holy in Isaiah 6 are the seraphim.

lessons.title: Seraphim Around the Throne
lessons.mainIdea: In Isaiah 6, seraphim with six wings stand above God's throne and call out that God is holy.
reading: Isaiah 6 begins in the year King Uzziah died. The prophet Isaiah has a vision of the Lord on a high throne. Above the throne stand *seraphim*. Each one has six wings. Two cover its face, two cover its feet, and with two it flies.

The seraphim call to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD." The doorposts shake, and the house fills with smoke. Isaiah feels he is not clean enough to be there. A seraph touches his lips with a hot coal from the altar. It tells him his guilt is taken away. Then Isaiah says, "Here I am. Send me."

The Hebrew word saraph seems to be linked to burning. The same word is used for the fiery serpents in Numbers 21:6. So some scholars, Heiser among them, think the seraphim may have looked like shining serpents. Other readers picture them in other ways. The text itself tells us only their wings and their words.

words.d: six-winged beings above God's throne in Isaiah 6; the word is the plural of seraph
something a prophet sees that God shows him, as Isaiah does in Isaiah 6

look.title: The Six Wings of a Seraph
look.prompt: Four of the six wings are used for covering. What might covering the face and feet show about standing near God?

check.q: How many wings does each seraph have in Isaiah 6?
check.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings: two over the face, two over the feet, two for flying.

check.q: What does a seraph touch to Isaiah's lips?
choices: A hot coal from the altar
check.why: In Isaiah 6, a seraph touches Isaiah's lips with a coal. The scroll to eat comes from the book of Ezekiel.

check.q: What do the seraphim call out to one another?
choices: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD
check.why: The seraphim call out Holy, holy, holy. Here I am, send me is what Isaiah says afterward.

lessons.title: Michael the Great Prince
lessons.mainIdea: Michael is named in Daniel, Jude and Revelation; Daniel calls him a great prince who stands up for Daniel's people.
reading: Only a few angels in the Bible have names. One is Michael. His name means "Who is like God?" Michael first appears in the Book of Daniel. In Daniel 10:13, a heavenly messenger tells Daniel that Michael came to help him.

Daniel 12:1 calls Michael "the great prince" who stands up for Daniel's people. A *prince* here means a leader or ruler. Heiser read these verses beside Deuteronomy 32:8. He thought they show heavenly beings who had charge over nations, with Michael caring for Israel.

Michael appears in the New Testament too. The letter of Jude, verse 9, calls him "the *archangel*." That means a chief messenger, a leader among angels. Revelation 12:7 pictures Michael leading the angels on God's side in a struggle in heaven.

words.d: a chief messenger or leader among angels; Jude 9 uses this title for Michael
in the Book of Daniel, a leader or ruler, used for Michael and for other heavenly beings

look.title: Where Michael Is Named
look.prompt: Which book names Michael most often? What kind of book is it, and why might that matter?

check.q: What does the name Michael mean?
check.why: Michael means Who is like God? God heals is the meaning of Raphael.

check.q: Which New Testament letter calls Michael the archangel?
check.why: Jude, verse 9, calls Michael the archangel. The other books are not New Testament letters.

check.q: How does Daniel 12:1 describe Michael?
choices: A great prince who stands up for Daniel's people
A messenger sent to Mary in Nazareth
A guard at the garden of Eden
check.why: Daniel 12:1 calls Michael the great prince who stands up for Daniel's people.

lessons.title: Gabriel Brings News
lessons.mainIdea: Gabriel explains visions to Daniel and brings news of coming births to Zechariah and to Mary.
reading: The other angel named in the Hebrew Bible is Gabriel. In Daniel 8:16, a voice tells Gabriel to help Daniel understand a vision. In Daniel 9:21, Gabriel comes to Daniel again in the evening. He comes to give Daniel wisdom and understanding.

Gabriel appears again in Luke 1. First he comes to Zechariah, a priest, inside the temple. He says Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth will have a son, John. He introduces himself: "I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God" (Luke 1:19).

Six months later, Gabriel is sent to Nazareth. He brings news to a young woman named Mary. He tells her she will have a son named Jesus. To Zechariah and to Mary, Gabriel's first words are the same: "Do not be afraid." His job fits the word mal'ak. He *announces* news and explains it.

words.d: to tell people important news, as Gabriel does in Luke 1
the town in Galilee where Luke says Gabriel visited Mary

look.title: Gabriel Then and Later
look.text: Daniel 9:21–22: While Daniel is praying in the evening, Gabriel comes to him and says he has come to give him understanding. Luke 1:19: Gabriel tells Zechariah, I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to bring you this good news.
look.prompt: Compare the two visits. What does Gabriel do both times? How does his job match the meaning of the word angel?

check.q: To whom does Gabriel bring news in Luke 1?
check.why: In Luke 1, Gabriel visits Zechariah in the temple and Mary in Nazareth.

check.q: What does Gabriel do for Daniel?
choices: Touches his lips with a coal
check.why: Daniel 8:16 and 9:21–22 show Gabriel giving Daniel understanding.

check.q: What are Gabriel's first words to both Zechariah and Mary?
check.why: Luke 1:13 and 1:30 both begin with Do not be afraid.

lessons.title: Raphael in the Book of Tobit
lessons.mainIdea: Raphael is named in the Book of Tobit, which is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament.
reading: A third named angel, Raphael, appears in the Book of Tobit. Tobit tells of a Jewish family living far from home in Nineveh. The son, Tobias, must make a long trip. A kind stranger offers to guide him. The stranger says his name is Azarias. A dog comes along too.

On the trip, the guide helps the family in many ways, and the story ends with healing. At the end, the guide tells them who he really is. "I am Raphael," he says, one of seven holy angels who stand before the Lord (Tobit 12:15). The name Raphael means "God heals."

Not every Bible has Tobit. It is in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. It is not in the Hebrew Bible. Protestants place it in a separate group called the *Apocrypha*, outside their *canon*. The book of 1 Enoch also names Raphael, alongside Michael and Gabriel.

words.d: the list of books a tradition accepts as its Bible
books, like Tobit, that Protestants keep outside their canon but that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include

look.title: The Guide Tells His Name
look.text: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels. We bring the prayers of God's people before him, and we go in and out before the glory of the Holy One.
look.cite: Tobit 12:15, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version Apocrypha (1611)
look.prompt: Raphael kept his real name secret for the whole trip. How does his job in the story fit his name, God heals?

check.q: What name does Raphael use while he guides Tobias?
check.why: In the Book of Tobit, the guide calls himself Azarias. He reveals he is Raphael near the end.

check.q: Which Bibles include Tobit in the Old Testament?
check.why: Tobit is in Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments. Protestants place it in the Apocrypha, and it is not in the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: What does the name Raphael mean?
check.why: Raphael means God heals. Who is like God? is the meaning of Michael.

lessons.title: Where Baby Angels Came From
lessons.mainIdea: Chubby baby angels come from art made long after the Bible; Bible angels often look like grown men and make people afraid.
reading: About five hundred years ago, painters in Italy liked to fill their pictures with little winged children. In art, these are often called *putti*. Around 1512, the painter Raphael put two small winged children at the bottom of a famous painting. People loved them. Over time, baby angels became a common picture.

The Bible describes angels very differently. In Genesis 18, three visitors come to Abraham. The text calls them men. In Genesis 19, two of them are called angels. Hebrews 13:2 says some people have welcomed angels as guests without knowing it. So angels in the Bible often look like grown people.

When angels show their glory, people are often afraid. That is why so many visits start with "Do not be afraid" (Luke 1:13; 1:30; 2:10). Heiser wanted readers to see this. Bible angels are strong and bright, not cute. Baby angels are art, not Bible description.

words.d: little winged children painted in European art, especially from about 1400 to 1700
great brightness and greatness; the Bible often links it to God and to God's messengers

look.title: Ornament and Text
look.text: On one side: a tree ornament of a chubby baby with tiny wings and a sweet smile. On the other side: Luke 2:9, where an angel stands before shepherds at night, God's glory shines all around them, and they are terrified.
look.prompt: List two ways the ornament and the story in Luke are different. Where did each picture come from?

check.q: Where did the picture of chubby baby angels mostly come from?
choices: Paintings made long after the Bible
check.why: Painters in Italy about five hundred years ago made winged children popular. The Bible does not describe angels that way.

check.q: In Genesis 18, how do the visitors to Abraham look?
check.why: Genesis 18:2 calls the visitors men. In Genesis 19:1, two of them are called angels.

check.q: Why do so many angel visits begin with Do not be afraid?
choices: The angels are about to leave
The angels are speaking to animals
People are often frightened when angels appear
check.why: In Luke, people are frightened by the angels' glory, so the angels start by calming them.

lessons.title: People Do Not Become Angels
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible never says people become angels when they die; angels and people are different kinds of beings.
reading: Many people call a loved one who has died "an angel." It is a loving way to talk. But Heiser, like many Bible scholars, pointed out that no verse says people turn into angels. In the Bible, angels and people are two different kinds of beings.

In Matthew 22:30, Jesus is asked a tricky question about marriage. He says that in the *resurrection*, people will not marry. They will be like the angels in heaven. Being like angels in one way is not the same as becoming angels.

Hebrews 12:22–23 gives a picture of a great gathering. It lists angels in one group. It lists the spirits of good people in another group. Christians hold many beliefs about what happens after death. But the Bible's own words keep angels and people separate.

words.d: being raised to life again after death, a hope described in the New Testament
a living someone; people are one kind of being, and angels are another

look.title: Like the Angels
look.text: In the resurrection, people do not marry, and they are not given in marriage. They are like the angels of God in heaven.
look.cite: Matthew 22:30, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The verse says like the angels. How is being like someone different from becoming that someone?

check.q: What did Heiser point out about people and angels?
choices: People become angels when they die
No verse says people turn into angels
Angels become people when they are born
People and angels are the same thing
check.why: Heiser, like many scholars, noted that the Bible never says people become angels.

check.q: In Matthew 22:30, what does Jesus say about people in the resurrection?
choices: They will guard the tree of life
They will be like the angels
check.why: Jesus says people will be like the angels in one way: they will not marry. He does not say they become angels.

check.q: How does Hebrews 12:22–23 list angels and good people?
check.why: Hebrews 12:22–23 names angels and the spirits of good people as different groups in one gathering.

lessons.title: Sent to Help
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as spirits who serve God and are sent to help people.
reading: Hebrews 1:14 sums up what angels do. It calls them spirits who serve. It says God sends them to help people who will receive salvation. Heiser's book Angels (2018) stresses this. Angels are *servants* of God, and they do what God sends them to do.

Bible stories show this help in plain ways. In 1 Kings 19:5–7, the prophet Elijah is worn out and asleep under a bush. An angel touches him and says, "Get up and eat." Bread and water are waiting. In Acts 12:7–10, an angel wakes Peter in prison. His chains fall off, and a gate opens by itself.

Angels in these stories point people to God, not to themselves. In Revelation 22:8–9, John bows down to an angel. The angel tells him not to. "I am a *fellow servant* with you," the angel says. "Worship God."

words.d: someone who works for another; Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as spirits who serve God
someone who serves the same master as you; the angel's words to John in Revelation 22:9

look.title: Spirits Who Serve
look.text: Are not all angels spirits who serve? God sends them out to help those who are going to receive salvation.
look.cite: Hebrews 1:14, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Name one Bible story from this lesson that fits this verse. Who was sent, and whom did they help?

check.q: How does Hebrews 1:14 describe angels?
choices: Spirits who serve and are sent to help
check.why: Hebrews 1:14 calls angels spirits who serve, sent to help people who will receive salvation.

check.q: What does the angel do for Elijah in 1 Kings 19?
choices: Opens a prison gate for him
Touches his lips with a coal
Wakes him and gives him food and water
check.why: In 1 Kings 19:5–7, the angel wakes Elijah and tells him to eat. The prison gate opens for Peter in Acts 12.

check.q: In Revelation 22:8–9, why does the angel stop John from bowing?
choices: The angel is a fellow servant, and John should worship God
The angel is late for another job
John is bowing to the wrong angel
Bowing is not allowed in Revelation
check.why: The angel says he is a fellow servant and tells John to worship God.

lessons.title: Eyes Opened at Dothan
lessons.mainIdea: In 2 Kings 6, Elisha's servant is shown horses and chariots of fire, a picture of the unseen world Heiser wrote about.
reading: In 2 Kings 6, the prophet Elisha is staying in the town of Dothan. One morning his servant wakes up early. An army with horses and chariots has surrounded the town. The servant is afraid. "What shall we do?" he asks.

Elisha tells him not to be afraid. He says, "Those who are with us are more than those who are with them." Then Elisha prays that the servant's eyes will be opened. The servant looks again. Now he sees the hills full of horses and *chariots* of fire all around Elisha (2 Kings 6:17).

Heiser named his big book The *Unseen Realm* (2015). He meant the world of God and heavenly beings that the Bible says is present but usually not seen. In this story, that world was there the whole time. The servant simply could not see it until his eyes were opened.

words.d: a two-wheeled cart pulled by horses, used in ancient armies
Heiser's name for the world of God and heavenly beings that the Bible describes as present but usually not seen

look.title: The Servant Sees
look.text: Elisha prayed, LORD, please open his eyes so that he can see. The LORD opened the young man's eyes. He saw that the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
look.cite: 2 Kings 6:17, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What changed in this verse: the hills, or what the servant could see? How does that fit the title The Unseen Realm?

check.q: What does Elisha's servant see after his eyes are opened?
check.why: 2 Kings 6:17 says the servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

check.q: Where is Elisha staying in this story?
check.why: 2 Kings 6:13 places Elisha in Dothan. Nazareth is Mary's town, and Nineveh is where Tobit's family lived.

check.q: What did Heiser mean by the unseen realm?
choices: The world of God and heavenly beings, present but usually not seen
A place people go when they dream
check.why: Heiser used the phrase for the Bible's world of God and heavenly beings, which the text says is near but usually unseen.

review.q: The English word angel comes from which Greek word?
review.why: Angel comes from the Greek angelos, which means messenger. Mal'ak is the Hebrew word.

review.q: Why did Heiser say angel is a job description?
choices: All angels have the same shape
Angels are paid for their work
Mal'ak and angelos mean messenger, which is what someone does
The word was invented by painters
review.why: Both the Hebrew and Greek words mean messenger. They describe a task, not a kind of being.

review.q: Which beings guard the path to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24?
review.why: Genesis 3:24 says God placed cherubim with a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

review.q: In which book does Isaiah see six-winged seraphim?
review.why: Isaiah 6 describes seraphim with six wings above the Lord's throne.

review.q: Which named angel appears in the Book of Tobit?
review.why: Raphael guides Tobias in the Book of Tobit. Micaiah is a human prophet in 1 Kings 22.

review.q: Which angel tells Zechariah, I stand in the presence of God?
review.why: Gabriel says this in Luke 1:19 when he announces the birth of John.

review.q: What does the Bible say happens to people when they die?
choices: It says they become babies with wings
It never says they become angels
It says they join the seraphim
review.why: No verse says people become angels. Hebrews 12:22–23 lists angels and people as separate groups.

review.q: Which verse calls angels spirits who serve, sent to help?
review.why: Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as serving spirits sent to help people.

chapters.title: The Angel of the LORD
chapters.bigQuestion: Who is the Angel of the LORD who speaks as God, and how have different readers understood him?

story.title: A Stranger Under the Oak
story.kicker: A young farmer hiding his wheat hears himself called a mighty warrior.
paragraphs: The Book of Judges tells of a hard time in Israel. Raiders from Midian swept in at every harvest. They took the crops and the animals. So people hid their food wherever they could. A young man named Gideon had some wheat. He did not dare work it out in the open.

Gideon took his wheat down into a winepress. A winepress was a low stone pit for squeezing grapes. It was an odd place to beat wheat, but it was hidden. Nearby stood an oak tree in the town of Ophrah. It belonged to Gideon's father, Joash (Judges 6:11).

A stranger was sitting under that oak. The text calls him the angel of the LORD. He looked at Gideon, crouched down in the pit, and spoke. "The LORD is with you, you mighty warrior" (Judges 6:12). Gideon did not feel mighty at all.

Gideon answered with honest questions. If the LORD was with them, why was life so hard? Then something strange happens in the story. The text stops saying the angel spoke. It says, "The LORD turned to him" and told him to go and save Israel (Judges 6:14).

Readers have wondered about this moment for a very long time. Who was the stranger under the oak? Was he a messenger speaking for God, or was he God himself, seen in a form Gideon could look at? This chapter follows that question through several Bible stories.
story.think: Why do you think the stranger calls Gideon a mighty warrior while Gideon is hiding in a pit?

sections.title: A Messenger Who Speaks as God

lessons.title: Hagar at the Spring
lessons.mainIdea: In Genesis 16, the angel of the LORD makes promises in God's own voice, and Hagar names the one who spoke to her God.
reading: Hagar was an Egyptian servant in the household of Abram and Sarai. Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away into the desert. The *angel of the LORD* found her by a spring of water on the road to Shur (Genesis 16:7). He asked where she was going.

The angel told Hagar to go back. Then he said, "I will greatly multiply your descendants." He did not say God will do it. He said I will. He told her to name her son Ishmael, which means "God hears." The LORD, he said, had heard her pain.

Genesis 16:13 then says that Hagar named "the LORD who spoke to her." She called him "the God who sees me." So the text calls the speaker both the angel of the LORD and the LORD. Heiser saw this as an important clue. Many other readers see it too.

words.d: a figure in the Hebrew Bible who is sent by God but often speaks as God
the name of Hagar's son; it means God hears

look.title: The God Who Sees
look.text: Hagar gave a name to the LORD who spoke to her. She called him, You are the God who sees me. For she said, Here I have seen the one who sees me.
look.cite: Genesis 16:13, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Verse 7 calls the speaker the angel of the LORD. Who does verse 13 say spoke to Hagar? What do you notice?

check.q: Where does the angel of the LORD find Hagar?
choices: By a spring of water in the desert
Under an oak tree in Ophrah
check.why: Genesis 16:7 says the angel found Hagar by a spring on the road to Shur.

check.q: What does the name Ishmael mean?
check.why: The angel says to name the boy Ishmael because the LORD has heard Hagar's pain (Genesis 16:11).

check.q: What is surprising about the angel's words in Genesis 16:10?
choices: He says I will, speaking as God
check.why: The angel says I will greatly multiply your descendants, a promise in God's own voice.

lessons.title: A Voice From Heaven to Abraham
lessons.mainIdea: In Genesis 22, the angel of the LORD calls to Abraham and says you have not held back your son from me.
reading: Genesis 22 tells a hard story. The text says God tested Abraham. God asked him to offer his son Isaac on a mountain. Readers in every tradition have found this story difficult. Jewish tradition calls it the *Akedah*, which means the binding.

Abraham went to the mountain. Before he could harm Isaac, the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven. "Abraham, Abraham!" the angel said. "Do not lay your hand on the boy" (Genesis 22:11–12). Then Abraham saw a ram caught in a bush and offered it instead.

Look closely at the angel's words. He says, "Now I know that you fear God. You have not held back your son from me." From me, not from God who sent me. In verse 16 the angel adds, "By myself I have sworn, says the LORD." Heiser pointed to verses like these. The messenger talks as God talks.

words.d: the Hebrew name, meaning the binding, that Jewish tradition gives to the story of Isaac in Genesis 22
a male sheep; in Genesis 22, Abraham offers a ram in place of Isaac

look.title: Who Is Speaking?
look.text: Genesis 22:11–12: The angel of the LORD calls from heaven. He says, Do not harm the boy. Now I know that you fear God, because you have not held back your son from me. Genesis 22:15–16: The angel of the LORD calls a second time and says, By myself I have sworn, says the LORD.
look.prompt: Find the words me and myself. Who is the angel talking about when he says them? Explain your answer from the verses.

check.q: Who stops Abraham in Genesis 22:11–12?
choices: The angel of the LORD, calling from heaven
check.why: Genesis 22:11 says the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven.

check.q: What does the angel say Abraham has not held back from him?
check.why: The angel says you have not held back your son from me, speaking as God.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition call the story in Genesis 22?
check.why: Akedah is the Hebrew name for the binding of Isaac. The Mishnah is a different Jewish book.

lessons.title: The Bush That Did Not Burn Up
lessons.mainIdea: In Exodus 3, the angel of the LORD appears in a flame, and then God speaks from the same bush.
reading: Moses was taking care of sheep near Mount Horeb. Exodus 3:2 says the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire. The fire came from the middle of a bush. The bush was burning, but it did not burn up. Moses turned aside to look.

Now read verse 4. "God called to him out of the middle of the bush." The angel appeared in the bush, and God spoke from the bush. God told Moses to take off his sandals, because the ground was *holy*. God said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob."

Moses hid his face. He was afraid to look at God (Exodus 3:6). Heiser read this as one more place where the angel and God are the same figure. Many Jewish readers explain it as God speaking through his messenger. Both readings start from the same words in the text.

words.d: set apart for God; in Exodus 3 the ground near the bush is holy
a mountain in Exodus, also called Sinai, where Moses saw the burning bush

look.title: From the Middle of the Bush
look.text: God called to Moses from the middle of the bush: Moses, Moses! Moses answered, Here I am. God said, Take off your sandals. The place where you stand is holy ground. I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Moses hid his face.
look.cite: Exodus 3:4–6, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Exodus 3:2 says the angel of the LORD appeared in the bush. Who speaks from the bush in these verses?

check.q: What was unusual about the bush in Exodus 3?
choices: It burned but did not burn up
check.why: Exodus 3:2 says the bush was burning, yet it was not burned up.

check.q: Who calls to Moses from the bush in Exodus 3:4?
check.why: Verse 2 says the angel of the LORD appeared in the flame, and verse 4 says God called from the bush.

check.q: How do many Jewish readers explain the angel in the bush?
check.why: Many Jewish readers see the angel as a messenger through whom God speaks. Heiser read the angel as God himself, seen.

lessons.title: The LORD Turned to Him
lessons.mainIdea: In Judges 6, the text first says the angel of the LORD spoke to Gideon and then says the LORD spoke to him.
reading: Judges 6 opens during hard years. Raiders from Midian kept taking Israel's crops. Gideon was beating out wheat in a winepress to hide it. The angel of the LORD sat under an oak nearby. He said, "The LORD is with you, you mighty warrior" (Judges 6:12).

Gideon asked a bold question. If the LORD is with us, why is all this happening? Then verse 14 says, "The LORD turned to him." The LORD told Gideon to go in his strength and *rescue* Israel. The writer moves from the angel to the LORD without a pause.

Gideon said his family was the weakest in his tribe. He said he was the youngest in his family. The answer came: "I will be with you" (Judges 6:16). Heiser noted how the text slides between the two names. To him, this showed the angel and the LORD as one.

words.d: a low stone pit for squeezing grapes; Gideon used one to hide his wheat
to save someone from danger or trouble; Gideon is told to rescue Israel from Midian

look.title: Angel, Then LORD
look.text: Verse 12: The angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, The LORD is with you, mighty warrior. Verse 14: The LORD turned to him and said, Go in this strength of yours and save Israel. Have I not sent you?
look.cite: Judges 6:12 and 6:14, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Who speaks in verse 12? Who speaks in verse 14? Is it the same speaker? Give a reason from the verses.

check.q: Where was Gideon beating out his wheat?
check.why: Judges 6:11 says Gideon beat out wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.

check.q: What does the angel call Gideon?
check.why: In Judges 6:12 the angel says, The LORD is with you, you mighty warrior.

check.q: What changes between Judges 6:12 and 6:14?
choices: Gideon moves to a different town
The text says the LORD is speaking instead of the angel
check.why: Verse 12 says the angel spoke; verse 14 says the LORD turned to Gideon and spoke.

lessons.title: Fire From the Rock
lessons.mainIdea: Gideon's offering burns up when the angel touches it, and Gideon names his altar The LORD Is Peace.
reading: Gideon asked for a sign. He brought out a meal of goat meat and flat bread. The angel of God told him to set it on a rock. The angel touched the food with the tip of his staff. Fire came up from the rock and burned it all. Then the angel was gone (Judges 6:19–21).

Gideon was afraid. "I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!" he cried. In the Bible, seeing God was thought to be very dangerous. But the LORD said to him, "Peace to you. Do not be afraid. You will not die" (Judges 6:23).

Gideon built an *altar* there. He named it "The LORD Is Peace" (Judges 6:24). The story ends calmly. Gideon is worried because he saw the angel. Heiser and other readers note that the worry makes most sense if seeing the angel was like seeing God.

words.d: a raised place made of stone or earth where gifts were offered to God
a long walking stick; the angel touches Gideon's food with the tip of his staff

look.title: Five Visits in This Chapter
look.cite: Counts of the verses in each passage as this chapter reads them
look.prompt: Which visit takes the most verses to tell? What happens in that story that might need more room?

check.q: What happens when the angel touches Gideon's food with his staff?
choices: Fire comes up from the rock and burns it
The food multiplies to feed an army
check.why: Judges 6:21 says fire rose from the rock and burned up the meat and bread.

check.q: Why is Gideon afraid after the angel leaves?
choices: He has seen the angel of the LORD face to face
check.why: Judges 6:22 says Gideon cried out because he had seen the angel of the LORD face to face.

check.q: What name does Gideon give his altar?
check.why: Judges 6:24 says Gideon called the altar The LORD Is Peace. The God Who Sees Me is Hagar's name in Genesis 16.

lessons.title: A Name Too Wonderful
lessons.mainIdea: In Judges 13, the angel who visits Samson's parents will not give his name, and they say they have seen God.
reading: Judges 13 tells of a couple from the town of Zorah. The husband was Manoah. His wife is not named. They had no children. The angel of the LORD came to her and said she would have a son. That son grew up to be Samson.

Manoah asked the visitor his name. The angel answered, "Why do you ask my name? It is *wonderful*" (Judges 13:18). Some translations say secret. Manoah offered a young goat on a rock. As the flame went up, the angel went up in the flame. Then Manoah knew he was the angel of the LORD.

Manoah said, "We will surely die, for we have seen God." His wife answered calmly. If the LORD meant to harm us, she said, he would not have accepted our gift or told us all this (Judges 13:22–23). Heiser pointed out that Manoah says they saw God, not just a messenger.

words.d: too amazing to understand; the angel's word for his own name in Judges 13:18
the town of Manoah and his wife, Samson's parents, in Judges 13

look.title: Manoah's Wife Answers
look.text: Manoah said to his wife, We will surely die, because we have seen God. But his wife said to him, If the LORD wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted our offering. He would not have shown us all these things or told us this news.
look.cite: Judges 13:22–23, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: How does Manoah's wife calm him? What reasons does she give from what they saw?

check.q: How does the angel answer when Manoah asks his name?
choices: He says it is wonderful, or secret
He says his name is Gabriel
He says his name is Michael
He writes it on the rock
check.why: Judges 13:18 says the angel asked why Manoah wanted his name and called it wonderful, or secret.

check.q: How does the angel leave Manoah and his wife?
choices: He walks away down the road
He goes up in the flame of the offering
He rides a chariot of fire
check.why: Judges 13:20 says the angel went up in the flame from the altar.

check.q: Who calms Manoah when he fears they will die?
check.why: Manoah's wife reasons that the LORD accepted their gift and told them good news (Judges 13:23).

lessons.title: My Name Is in Him
lessons.mainIdea: In Exodus 23:20–21, God says his name is in the angel he sends ahead of Israel.
reading: In Exodus 23, Israel is getting ready to travel to a new land. God says, "I am sending an angel ahead of you." The angel will guard them on the way. He will bring them to the place God has prepared (Exodus 23:20).

Then God gives a warning. Listen to him, and do not rebel against him. "He will not pardon your wrongdoing, for my *name* is in him" (Exodus 23:21). In the Bible, a name is more than a label. It stands for who someone is.

Heiser thought this verse was very important. In the Hebrew Bible, forgiving wrongdoing belongs to God. And God's name was in this angel. For Heiser, that meant the angel carried God's own presence. Other readers say the angel simply carried God's *authority*, the way an ambassador speaks for a king.

words.d: in the Bible, more than a label; a name stands for who someone is
the right to speak or act for someone, as an ambassador speaks for a ruler

look.title: An Angel Sent Ahead
look.text: I am sending an angel ahead of you, to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared. Pay attention to him and listen to his voice. Do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your wrongdoing, because my name is in him.
look.cite: Exodus 23:20–21, paraphrased in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What does God say is in the angel? Explain what that could mean in two different ways.

check.q: What does God say is in the angel in Exodus 23:21?
check.why: Exodus 23:21 says, My name is in him.

check.q: Why did Heiser think Exodus 23:21 was important?
choices: It is the only verse about angels
The angel has God's name and deals with wrongdoing, which belongs to God
check.why: Heiser noted that the angel carries God's name and deals with pardon, which in the Hebrew Bible belongs to God.

check.q: How do other readers explain the angel in Exodus 23?
choices: He is a painting in the tabernacle
He is one of the Midianites
He carries God's authority, like an ambassador
check.why: Many readers see the angel as a messenger with God's authority, the way an ambassador speaks for a king.

lessons.title: God Unseen and God Seen
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the Angel of the LORD was God in a form people could see, a second figure he called a second Yahweh.
reading: Some verses say no one can see God. In Exodus 33:20, God tells Moses, "No one may see me and live." Yet Jacob says in Genesis 32:30, "I have seen God face to face." Hagar, Gideon and Manoah say much the same. How can both be true?

Heiser offered an answer in The Unseen Realm (2015). He said the Hebrew Bible shows God in two ways. One is God who is unseen, in heaven. The other is God who is seen, often as the Angel of the LORD. Heiser called this the *two Yahwehs* idea. *Yahweh* is the personal name of God in Hebrew.

Many English Bibles print that name as LORD in small capital letters. Many Jewish readers do not say the name aloud, out of respect. Heiser said Christians later linked the seen God with Jesus. He believed that link grew out of these Hebrew stories. Other readers disagree, as the next lessons show.

words.d: the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often printed LORD in English Bibles
Heiser's name for his reading: God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD

look.title: Two Verses Side by Side
look.text: Exodus 33:20: God tells Moses, You cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live. Genesis 32:30: After wrestling all night, Jacob names the place Peniel. He says, I have seen God face to face, and my life was spared.
look.prompt: These two verses seem to pull in different directions. How would Heiser's two Yahwehs reading explain both? How might a reader who disagrees explain them?

check.q: What did Heiser call his reading of the Angel of the LORD?
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser described God unseen and God seen as two Yahwehs.

check.q: Which verse says no one may see God and live?
check.why: Exodus 33:20 says no one may see God and live. Genesis 32:30 is where Jacob says he saw God face to face.

check.q: How is the name Yahweh often printed in English Bibles?
check.why: Many English Bibles print God's personal name as LORD in small capitals.

lessons.title: The Word and the Name
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser also pointed to verses where the Word of the LORD and the Name of the LORD seem to act like a person.
reading: Heiser noticed that the angel is not the only clue. Genesis 15:1 says "the *word of the LORD* came to Abram in a vision." A few verses later, this Word brings Abram outside and tells him to count the stars (Genesis 15:5). Heiser read this Word as someone Abram could see.

In 1 Samuel 3:10, the LORD "came and stood" and called the boy Samuel. Verse 21 says the LORD showed himself to Samuel "by the word of the LORD." Heiser read these as more pictures of God being seen. Other readers take word here to mean a message.

The Name works the same way. Deuteronomy 12:11 speaks of the place where God will make his name dwell. And in Exodus 23:21, God's name is in the angel. In Genesis 48:15–16, Jacob blesses his grandsons in the name of God and the angel who rescued him. Heiser noted that the verb bless there is singular.

words.d: a phrase for God's message; Heiser thought it sometimes names a figure people could see
about only one; a singular verb has one subject doing the action

look.title: The Word Comes and Stands
look.text: Genesis 15:1, 5: The word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision. He brought Abram outside and said, Look up and count the stars. 1 Samuel 3:10: The LORD came and stood there and called, Samuel, Samuel.
look.prompt: What do the Word and the LORD do in these verses that a person would do? Does that make you read word as a message or as someone who can be seen? Why?

check.q: In Genesis 15, what does the word of the LORD do after it comes to Abram?
choices: Brings him outside to count the stars
check.why: Genesis 15:5 says he brought Abram outside and told him to count the stars.

check.q: Which verse says God's name will dwell in a place he chooses?
check.why: Deuteronomy 12:11 speaks of the place where God will make his name dwell.

check.q: In Genesis 48:15–16, what did Heiser notice about the verb bless?
choices: It is in Greek, not Hebrew
It is singular, though God and the angel are both named
It is missing from the verse
check.why: Heiser noted the singular verb, as if God and the angel act as one to bless Jacob's grandsons.

lessons.title: A Messenger Speaking for God
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish readers usually read the Angel of the LORD as a messenger who speaks with God's authority, the way an agent stands for the one who sent him.
reading: Jewish readers have usually read these stories another way. They see the angel of the LORD as a messenger. A messenger may speak in the first person for the one who sent him. A royal herald could read a king's letter aloud and say I, meaning the king.

The Mishnah is a collection of Jewish teaching written down about 200 CE. It states a rule about an *agent*. An agent is someone sent to act for another person. The Mishnah says a person's agent is like the person himself (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). Readers use this idea to explain why an angel can say I will for God.

Some ancient Jewish teachers argued about a teaching called *two powers in heaven*. Later rabbis rejected it. They held that there is one God, with no second power beside him. Heiser studied these old arguments. He thought they showed that some Jewish readers once saw two figures in these stories.

words.d: someone sent to act or speak for another person
a collection of Jewish teaching and law, written down about 200 CE
an idea, debated in ancient times and later rejected by the rabbis, that a second divine figure stood beside God

look.title: An Agent Is Like the Sender
look.text: A person's agent is like the person himself.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 5:5, c. 200 CE, paraphrased in simple words
look.prompt: How could this rule explain an angel who says I will when he makes God's promise to Hagar?

check.q: How do Jewish readers usually understand the angel of the LORD?
choices: As a messenger who speaks with God's authority
As a cherub on the ark
check.why: Jewish readers usually see the angel as a messenger or agent speaking for God, not as God himself.

check.q: According to Mishnah Berakhot 5:5, what is a person's agent like?
choices: Like a servant who must stay silent
check.why: The Mishnah teaches that a person's agent is like the person himself.

check.q: What did later rabbis decide about two powers in heaven?
choices: They made it their main teaching
They rejected it and held there is one God
They said it came from Tobit
check.why: Later rabbis rejected the two powers teaching and held to one God with no second power.

lessons.title: Christians and the Angel
lessons.mainIdea: Many early Christians linked the Angel of the LORD with Jesus, while others, like Augustine, thought God spoke through created angels.
reading: About 155 CE, a Christian writer named Justin Martyr wrote a long debate. It is called Dialogue with Trypho. Justin talked about the one who appeared to Abraham, Jacob and Moses. He argued that this was the one Christians call the Son of God. Many early Christian writers read the stories that way.

The Gospel of John says, "No one has ever seen God" (John 1:18). It says that God the only Son has made him known. John 1:14 says the *Word* became flesh and lived among people. Heiser pointed to these verses. He thought John was building on the Hebrew stories of God seen.

Not all Christians agree. Augustine, a North African bishop writing about 400 CE, took a careful view. He thought God may have spoken through created angels in some of these stories. So readers differ within traditions too. Each reading starts from the same Bible passages.

words.d: in John 1, a title Christians use for Jesus; Heiser linked it to the word of the LORD in the Hebrew Bible
a leader of Christian churches in a city or region

look.title: Readers Through the Years
look.cite: Common scholarly dates for each work; Heiser, The Divine Council (2004) and The Unseen Realm (2015)
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Justin Martyr and Heiser's The Unseen Realm? What does that tell you about how long this question has been asked?

check.q: Who linked the one who appeared to Abraham and Moses with the Son of God, about 155 CE?
check.why: Justin Martyr made this argument in his Dialogue with Trypho, about 155 CE.

check.q: What did Augustine think about some of these stories?
choices: The stories were written by Heiser
God may have spoken through created angels
The angel was a person who died
check.why: Augustine, about 400 CE, thought God may have spoken through created angels in some appearances.

check.q: Which verse says the Word became flesh and lived among people?
check.why: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Heiser linked this to the word of the LORD in the Hebrew Bible.

review.q: Where did Gideon meet the angel of the LORD?
choices: By a winepress, near an oak in Ophrah
By a spring on the road to Shur
At a burning bush on Mount Horeb
review.why: Judges 6:11 places the angel under the oak at Ophrah while Gideon worked in the winepress.

review.q: Hagar names the one who spoke to her. What name does she use?
review.why: Genesis 16:13 says Hagar called the LORD who spoke to her the God who sees me.

review.q: In which passage does the angel appear in a flame and God speak from a bush?
review.why: Exodus 3:2–4 tells of the angel in the flame and God calling to Moses from the bush.

review.q: What is Heiser's two Yahwehs reading?
choices: God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD
Two angels named Michael and Gabriel
Two books of the Bible about angels
review.why: Heiser argued the Hebrew Bible shows God unseen and God seen, and Christians later linked the seen God to Jesus.

review.q: What does Exodus 23:21 say about the angel God sends ahead of Israel?
choices: He is a baby with wings
review.why: Exodus 23:21 says, My name is in him, a verse Heiser found very important.

review.q: How do Jewish readers usually explain an angel who speaks as God?
choices: He is an agent speaking for the one who sent him
He is a person who died
review.why: Jewish readers usually read the angel as a messenger or agent, and the Mishnah says an agent is like the sender.

review.q: Who reassures Manoah that they will not die?
review.why: In Judges 13:23, Manoah's wife points out that the LORD accepted their gift and told them good news.

review.q: Which early Christian writer linked these appearances to the Son of God?
review.why: Justin Martyr, about 155 CE, argued that the one who appeared to Abraham and Moses was the Son of God.
